clinicalPearls: A group of inherited platelet secretion defects caused by deficiency of dense (delta) granules, alpha granules, or both, producing mild to moderate mucocutaneous bleeding
Typical features are easy bruising, epistaxis, menorrhagia, and prolonged bleeding after surgery or dental procedures despite a normal platelet count
Dense-granule deficiency can be part of syndromic disorders such as Hermansky-Pudlak (with oculocutaneous albinism) and Chediak-Higashi syndrome
Alpha-granule deficiency defines gray platelet syndrome, in which platelets appear large and agranular (gray) on the blood film with a tendency to progressive myelofibrosis
Light transmission aggregometry classically shows an absent secondary wave and impaired response to weak agonists, with a blunted ATP release
The platelet count is usually normal or only mildly reduced, so the defect is qualitative rather than quantitative
Management centres on avoiding antiplatelet drugs, using antifibrinolytics and local measures, and reserving platelet transfusion for significant bleeding or surgery
reference.pathophysiology: Platelet storage pool disease reflects a failure to form, fill, or release the contents of platelet secretory granules. Dense (delta) granules store ADP, ATP, calcium, and serotonin, which amplify platelet activation and recruitment; their deficiency blunts the secondary aggregation response. Alpha granules store adhesive and procoagulant proteins including von Willebrand factor, fibrinogen, and platelet factor 4, and their absence in gray platelet syndrome impairs platelet function and is associated with marrow fibrosis. The resulting defective granule release weakens the platelet activation amplification loop and produces a mucocutaneous bleeding tendency.
additionalDifferentials: Aspirin or other antiplatelet drug effect
Acquired platelet dysfunction from uraemia or myeloproliferative disease
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film to assess platelet number and morphology (gray, agranular platelets)
Light transmission platelet aggregometry with weak and strong agonists
Dense-granule ATP release (lumiaggregometry) or nucleotide content measurement
Whole-mount electron microscopy to enumerate dense granules
Von Willebrand factor studies to exclude von Willebrand disease
Genetic testing for syndromic forms such as Hermansky-Pudlak or gray platelet syndrome
redFlags: Severe or unexpected perioperative or postpartum haemorrhage
Bleeding compounded by inadvertent antiplatelet drug use
Features of a syndromic disorder such as albinism or recurrent infections suggesting a broader diagnosis
Progressive cytopenias or splenomegaly suggesting marrow fibrosis in gray platelet syndrome
reference.prognosis: Most patients have a mild, manageable bleeding tendency compatible with a normal life when antiplatelet agents are avoided and procedures are covered. Prognosis is modified by any associated syndrome, and gray platelet syndrome may progress to clinically significant myelofibrosis.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis because the platelet count is normal
Missing an underlying syndrome such as Hermansky-Pudlak by not examining for albinism
Attributing aggregation abnormalities to recent antiplatelet drug use without a proper drug-free interval
Failing to give perioperative haemostatic cover for an apparently mild disorder
references: Hoffman: Hematology - Basic Principles and Practice
